title: Vinho Verde
description: Portugal's green north-west: light, fresh whites and the serious Alvarinho of Monção e Melgaço.
L: Explain the meaning of its name

Vinho Verde covers the Minho, Portugal's green north-west, between the Minho river, on the Spanish border, and the Douro, and from the Atlantic inland. It's Portugal's largest DOC, about 21,000 hectares, divided into nine sub-regions, like Monção e Melgaço, Lima, Cávado and Basto. Granite soils dominate.

The climate is Atlantic: mild, humid and wet, often 1,200 to 2,000 mm of rain a year. That keeps the landscape green and the grapes fresh, but brings disease. Traditionally, vines grew high on trees, pergolas and tall trellises, called enforcado and ramada, letting air circulate and leaving land below for food crops.
Why were Vinho Verde vines traditionally trained high?
To let air circulate and free land below for crops
Height reduced rot and allowed farming underneath.

Verde means green, but it refers to youth, not colour: the wine is drunk young and fresh. The name also echoes the region's green landscape. Vinho Verde can be white, red or rosé, though white dominates today. The DOC was demarcated in 1908.
Verde means young, not green in colour
Vinho Verde means the wine is green in colour.
Not true. Verde refers to youth and freshness, and to the green landscape.
Vinho Verde is Portugal's largest DOC, in the green north-west
Its Atlantic climate is wet and humid
Verde means young and fresh, not green in colour

Alvarinho, the same as Spain's Albariño, gives the fullest, most aromatic wines, especially in Monção e Melgaço. Loureiro gives floral, laurel-scented, citrus wines, mainly in Lima. Arinto, called Pedernã here, gives crisp, lemony acidity. Avesso, in Baião, gives fuller, nuttier wines. Trajadura adds body and softness.

Red Vinho Verde, mainly from Vinhão, is deeply coloured, tart and tannic, traditionally served chilled in white bowls with grilled sardines; it's popular locally but rare abroad. Most white Vinho Verde is light, about 9 to 11.5% alcohol, crisp, often with a slight spritz from added carbon dioxide. Single-grape and single-estate wines are more serious.
Match each grape to its character.
Vinho Verde's grapes each bring something different.
A traditional Vinho Verde's slight spritz once came from malolactic fermentation in bottle; today most producers add carbon dioxide.
What is Alvarinho called in Spain?
The same grape across the Minho river.
Alvarinho, Loureiro, Arinto and Avesso are the key whites
Most Vinho Verde is light and slightly spritzy
Red Vinhão is a local, tart, dark speciality

Monção e Melgaço is the northernmost sub-region, along the south bank of the Minho river, facing Spain's Rías Baixas. Hills to the west shelter it from Atlantic winds and rain, so it's warmer and drier in summer than the rest of Vinho Verde. Granite and alluvial soils dominate.

Monção e Melgaço is Alvarinho's heartland. Until 2021, it was the only sub-region allowed to label a wine Alvarinho on the front. The wines are fuller, riper and more aromatic than typical Vinho Verde, around 12.5 to 13.5%, with peach, citrus, tropical fruit and minerality, rarely spritzy. They can age five to ten years.
Why is Monção e Melgaço warmer than the rest of Vinho Verde?
Hills shelter it from Atlantic winds
Shelter makes it warmer and drier.

Producers make Alvarinho in several styles: fresh and unoaked, lees-aged for texture, oak-fermented, and even sparkling, Espumante. Soalheiro, founded in 1974, was a pioneer of quality Alvarinho here. Alvarinho Superior and single-vineyard wines show its potential.
Monção e Melgaço Alvarinho is usually light and spritzy.
Not true. It's fuller, riper and rarely spritzy.
Monção e Melgaço is sheltered and warmer
Its wines are fuller and can age five to ten years
Reading Vinho Verde and eating with it

Labels show Vinho Verde DOC, sometimes a sub-region like Monção e Melgaço or Lima, and often a grape: Alvarinho, Loureiro, Avesso. Regional wines may use Vinho Regional Minho. A sticker seal on the bottle certifies the DOC. Single-estate wines, from a quinta, are usually more serious than branded blends.

Vinho Verde suits light, fresh food: grilled sardines, clams, octopus, salads and sushi. Alvarinho suits richer seafood, bacalhau, grilled fish and white meat. Loureiro suits aperitifs and Asian food. Serve at 7 to 10 degrees. Most is best within a year; Alvarinho from Monção e Melgaço can age.
Which dish suits a light Vinho Verde?
Light, crisp wine suits simple grilled fish.
In Portugal's summer festivals, grilled sardines and chilled Vinho Verde are a classic combination.
Labels show the DOC, sub-region and often a grape
Vinho Verde suits sardines and seafood
Serve cold; most is best young
